POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 23:27:50 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.9 FlyDubai suspends flights to and from Israel after pilot stabbing https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/30/flydubai-flights-israel-pilot-stabbing-01101806?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 30 Sep 2026 23:27:42 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9089426 FlyDubai Airlines has suspended all its flights to and from Israel after one pilot stabbed another on a flight to Tel Aviv, causing the plane to plummet thousands of feet.

The Emirati flight made an emergency landing Wednesday in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after crew and passengers entered the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot, according to Israeli officials. A second pair of FlyDubai pilots were on board and able to land the plane, according to FlyDubai and Reuters.

All passengers arrived safely in Tel Aviv by Wednesday night after FlyDubai sent replacement aircrafts to Tabuk.

“This temporary suspension will allow the relevant authorities to continue their work and establish all the facts surrounding the incident,” said FlyDubai, one of the largest flight operators in the Middle East.

Flight FZ 1073 departed Dubai on Wednesday morning local time en route to Tel Aviv, an approximately four-hour trip. Approximately two hours into the flight, the plane made a steep descent, followed by a sharp ascent and another descent, according to Flightradar24, a flight tracking service. The plane plunged more than 15,000 feet in a span of two minutes, according to the radar.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement that the assailant “apparently attempted to crash the plane with its passengers on board.” Nearly all the passengers on the flight were Israeli, he said.

On social media, Netanyahu called the injured co-pilot, identified as Capt. Smit Machchhar, a “true hero” for opening the cockpit door and enabling passengers and crew to jump the assailant and secure the plane. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on X that Machchhar was hospitalized there in stable condition.

President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday that he spoke with Netanyahu about the attack and said the assailant appeared to be either “a terrorist or perhaps a whack job.”

Much of the details of the incident remain unclear as authorities investigate its cause.

The United Arab Emirates has had diplomatic relations with Israel since 2020, and the UAE government reportedly tried to warn Israel of a pending Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023. During the weekend, Netanyahu traveled to the UAE for discussions.

“We believe that, in the face of rising inflation caused by high global energy prices, it is necessary to grant member states additional flexibility to support households and businesses,” she said.

European countries are struggling with higher energy costs driven by the war in Iran, and fear that increased costs will put delicate growth at risk and stoke inflation.

]]> en L’UE accusée de dissimuler l’impact environnemental des datacenters https://www.politico.eu/article/lue-accusee-de-dissimuler-limpact-environnemental-des-datacenters/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:52:33 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9085379 Une plainte déposée lundi contre la Commission européenne dénonce l’opacité de l’UE sur la consommation d’énergie des centres de données.

Dans le détail, cette plainte déposée cette semaine par Lighthouse Reports, comme l’a révélé POLITICO, accuse l’exécutif européen d’avoir mis en place des règles empêchant le public de connaître la consommation d’énergie et d’eau de chaque datacenter.

Cette action en justice intervient alors que l’opposition ne cesse de croître à travers l’Europe contre ces centres de données énergivores, indispensables au fonctionnement de l’intelligence artificielle, et alors que les prix de l’énergie sont en hausse.

Lighthouse Reports, une ONG basée aux Pays-Bas qui mène des enquêtes dans plusieurs pays sur de potentiels méfaits commis par des gouvernements et des entreprises, accuse la Commission d’ériger un “mur du silence” autour de la question de la consommation d’énergie.

Les décideurs politiques de l’UE seraient déterminés “à refuser ou à dissuader l’accès aux informations relatives aux performances des centres de données, et à en brouiller la compréhension”, peut-on lire dans la plainte déposée au titre de la Convention d’Aarhus, un traité international juridiquement contraignant qui garantit au public le droit à l’information et à la participation aux décisions en matière d’environnement.

Cette procédure affrontera son premier test en novembre, lorsque le Comité d’examen du respect des dispositions de la Convention d’Aarhus se réunira pour statuer sur sa recevabilité. Par la suite, la Convention d’Aarhus pourrait conclure que l’UE a manqué aux obligations qui lui incombent en vertu du texte.

Contactée par POLITICO, la Commission n’a pas répondu à notre demande de commentaire.

Des gourmands en énergie

Alors que l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle entraîne une hausse de la demande énergétique, l’UE a officiellement annoncé son objectif de tripler la capacité de ses centres de données dans les années à venir, afin de rester dans la course face aux Etats-Unis et à la Chine. Parallèlement, face à la hausse des prix de l’énergie, la contestation citoyenne contre les centres de données prend de l’ampleur à travers l’Europe.

Afin de limiter l’impact environnemental, la Commission a présenté la semaine dernière un nouveau label de transparence destiné à orienter les investissements vers des installations plus respectueuses de l’environnement ; des normes minimales de performance devraient suivre.

“Si nous ne veillons pas à ce que ces grands consommateurs d’énergie respectent bel et bien nos objectifs généraux […] ils risquent alors de compromettre notre capacité à atteindre nos propres objectifs”, avait alors déclaré Dan Jørgensen, le commissaire européen chargé de l’Energie, dans une interview accordée à POLITICO.

Selon les chiffres de la Commission, les centres de données européens ont consommé 20,7 térawattheures d’électricité — soit à peu près autant que la consommation totale de la Croatie — et plus de 8 millions de mètres cubes d’eau en 2025. Cela représente une augmentation de 26% de la consommation d’électricité et de 52% de la consommation d’eau par rapport à 2024.

Mais ces chiffres ne reflètent pas complètement l’utilisation réelle du secteur, car ils résultent de données incomplètes recueillies par l’exécutif européen. Ces données n’ont été publiées que sous forme agrégée, conformément à une loi de 2024 interdisant à Bruxelles et aux Etats membres de divulguer “toutes les informations et tous les indicateurs clés de performance relatifs à chaque centre de données”, après un lobbying des géants de la tech, qui invoquaient des intérêts commerciaux.

Diego Solier, un député européen conservateur qui travaille au projet de législation européenne visant à renforcer les capacités numériques du continent, considère que l’expansion des datacenters en Europe doit s’accompagner d’informations fiables destinées aux citoyens et aux décideurs politiques concernant la consommation d’énergie et d’eau.

“La transparence devrait être le point de départ”, a estimé Diego Solier, qui n’a pas souhaité s’exprimer sur la plainte elle-même — elle n’avait pas encore été rendue publique. “En même temps, la transparence doit être proportionnée et ne devrait pas obliger les entreprises à divulguer des informations vraiment sensibles sur le plan commercial.”

Le droit de savoir

Selon Lighthouse Reports, la Commission “porte la responsabilité principale [d’avoir] empêché le public de prendre connaissance des effets de l’expansion massive des centres de données en Europe”, en permettant aux opérateurs de garder secrets les détails de leur consommation et d’échapper ainsi à tout droit de regard — en violation de la Convention d’Aarhus, ratifiée par l’UE en 2005.

Après avoir tenté en vain de contraindre la Commission et les gouvernements nationaux à divulguer les données dont ils disposent, Lighthouse Reports les accuse de se retrancher à tort derrière des clauses d’exemption.

“La Commission se trouve au sommet d’un système de non-divulgation qui englobe la grande majorité de l’UE”, écrit l’ONG. “Privilégier le secret commercial au détriment du droit de savoir des citoyens érode la légitimité et entame encore davantage la confiance.”

Les nouvelles mesures visant à renforcer la transparence, notamment un système de notation vivement critiqué par les organisations professionnelles, ne suffisent pas à redresser la barre, ajoute Lighthouse Reports.

A partir de l’été prochain, ce système imposera aux opérateurs d’évaluer leur efficacité énergétique, leur consommation d’eau et leur recours à l’énergie propre sur une échelle allant d’A à G. Cependant, l’ONG fait valoir que ces règles ne révèlent toujours pas la consommation énergétique totale ni d’autres indicateurs clés permettant d’évaluer correctement l’empreinte carbone de ces infrastructures.

“Le fait de privilégier les ratios plutôt que les chiffres réels de consommation ne repose sur aucune contrainte technique ; il s’agit d’un choix qui favorise les intérêts du secteur au détriment de l’intérêt général”, argumente Lighthouse Reports dans sa plainte.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Rutte’s unusually strong remarks underscore the growing tensions between Moscow and NATO countries as hybrid attacks and Russian-linked sabotage proliferate across Europe.

In recent days, Russia’s embassy in Belgium sent NATO a note alleging the alliance was displaying “reckless and irresponsible” behavior near its Kaliningrad exclave, following alliance exercises involving several reconnaissance planes, ground forces and fighter jets near the region, which is between Poland and Lithuania, last month.

“We have emphasised that Russia possesses the necessary means to repel any potential aggression and is prepared to deploy its entire arsenal to defend its territory should NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country,” the embassy wrote on social media.

In its letter to NATO, Moscow explicitly mentions the use of its nuclear arsenal and issues specific threats to hit allied territory, according to one NATO diplomat briefed on the letter, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.

NATO has sent a note back to Russian officials in response, the alliance’s spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed.

“We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia,” she said in a statement. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”

Inside NATO, some allies are dismissing the threat. “Our reading is that they want to intimidate allied public opinion so that allies stop supporting [Ukraine], while, at the same time, presenting NATO as the one that would be responsible for an eventual escalation,” said the same NATO diplomat cited above. “Textbook Russian propaganda.”

“Russia always accelerates when it’s the most guilty or when [it] loses,” said a second alliance diplomat. “So they are cornered now and they transfer the blame on NATO.”

Russia’s embassy to Belgium didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Belgians are pressing ahead with their own national version, putting civil liberties of everyone at risk. ]]> When we broke the story about police raids in the EU’s deportation bill last December, comparisons to Donald Trump’s paramilitary ICE anti-migrant forces were soon being made.

EU interior ministers on Thursday (1 October) in Luxembourg are now set to formally adopt the return regulation, which sets the legal framework for police to carry out raids and seize people’s “belongings, electronic devices, and other items of relevance.”

The logic is part of a maximalist effort to deport people, such as failed asylum seekers, back to their home countries or possibly even in yet-to-be defined transit centres in Rwanda or elsewhere.

The regulation targets anyone “for the purpose of preparing or ensuring an effective return” with raids being allowed in a “place of residence or other relevant premises.”

Although the item is but a mere footnote in Thursday’s agenda, the potential consequences of the law have roused alarm among civil rights organisations who continue to draw parallels with ICE.

The comparison is not alarmist.

Trump’s Minnesota threats couldn’t happen in Europe — could they?

]]> Where Russian maps place the occupiers, and where they really are — an overview of parts of the front (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,679) https://euobserver.com/240588/where-russian-maps-place-the-occupiers-and-where-they-really-are-an-overview-of-parts-of-the-front-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1679/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:54:44 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240588 Ukraine is losing the battle in the skies but holding strong on the battleground. And Russian media highlight “liberated” villages, but in reality they are still under Ukrainian control.]]>

  • The Ukrainian army stays in control of front lines, but safety in cities deteriorates.

  • Kyiv was on fire again as Russian attacks on cities intensify.
  • Rubikon published stats on destroyed Ukrainian drones, decoys being the second most prominent.
  • Russia’s defence ministry will not let go of the Armata: it wants to turn it into an air-defence system, drawing ridicule.
  • Maps of the day: Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction; Orikhiv direction, Oleksandrivsk direction, Kupiansk direction.
  • Videos of the day: a burning Tu-95MS strategic bomber; a Ukrainian firefighter showed how they extinguished the Academy of Sciences building.

    • The Ukrainian army stays in control of front lines, but safety in cities deteriorates. The war has reached a stage in which two separate conflicts appear to be taking place simultaneously.

    While Ukraine is currently losing the battle in the air and its cities are continually suffering missile and strikes by jet drones, the situation on battlefields is far better.

    Last week, Denník N spent time in Ukraine with former chief of the general staff Daniel Zmeko. During the trip, reporters met commanding officers from several brigades and battalions operating from the Izium area to Zaporizhzhia, and all of them said they had the situation under control.

    The officers spoke about the accuracy of Russian maps, which they said did not correspond to reality. In some places, Russian soldiers are as far as 20 km from the locations where, according to the Kremlin, they are supposed to be.

    Northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration: This is a specific section of the front where the Ukrainian army has been reporting its advances only very slowly, while Ukrainian analysts have remained silent so as not to disclose anything sensitive. Russian bloggers, by contrast, are depicting the situation more closely to reality.

    Yet official Russian maps persist with utterly nonsensical lines. We do not know to what extent this is an effort to deceive domestic and foreign audiences, and to what extent they genuinely believe it in Moscow. It is worth looking at how the regime wants the situation to appear, and what it is really like.

    The first map in the overview was produced by the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti and depicts the area around Lyman, on the northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction, as of 29 September. Lyman is shown as occupied in the middle of the map. The map’s author also continues to insist that the Russian army had captured Sviatohirsk — at the tip of the red salient in the centre of the map — and that Russia controls the entire, now non-existent salient with the village of Novoselivka at its centre. Yet Russian outlets Rybar and Two Majors write that fighting is taking place on the Zherebets river around the villages of Terny — on the far right of the map — and Yampil.

    The following map is much closer to reality. According to it, the front line roughly follows the Zherebets river, which corresponds to Rybar’s claims.

    Rybar’s map looks like this:

    Kupiansk direction: The city of Kupiansk is a similar case to Sviatohirsk. Putin declared it captured in August last year. And once the commander-in-chief had declared this, his news agency continued to draw the map as though it were true. Kupiansk is shown as occupied in its centre, but there are further inaccuracies.

    For example, the Kremlin agency claims that the Ukrainian bridgehead on the eastern bank of the Oskil river south of the city no longer exists. Ukrainians do face major difficulties supplying it, and various analysts have repeatedly warned of an impending disaster, but the Russian map is nevertheless hopelessly inaccurate.

    Also note the small town of Borova at the bottom centre. RIA Novosti also shows it as occupied, although this is not the case.

    This time, we will compare the Russian agency’s data with a map by Ukrainian analysts at DeepStateUA, because they updated it on Tuesday to reflect a new advance by Ukrainian units north of Kupiansk — again in the centre of the map — near the village of Dvorichne. In recent weeks, they have succeeded in reducing the Russian bridgehead on the western bank of the Oskil; the change since the end of August is marked in blue. Borova is again at the bottom centre, while below Kupiansk is the Ukrainian bridgehead that Russia claims does not exist.

    Orikhiv: This is one of the places where Ukrainian officers said during reporters’ trip to Ukraine that Russian maps were particularly inaccurate.

    The Russian map is again from RIA Novosti and again ignores reality along the entire length of this section of the front. Its main target is the city of Zaporizhzhia, with a population of three quarters of a million, in the centre left, while the small town of Orikhiv, at the bottom centre, is a defensive hub.

    Putin’s news agency places soldiers roughly 12 km from the southern edge of Zaporizhzhia; in reality, they are around 24 km away. It shows Orikhiv as occupied and the Russian army advancing from the east towards the village of Novorozivka, north of Orikhiv.

    The OSINT project Playfra covers this area in the greatest detail. Its map appears to depict a different war altogether. Everywhere, Russian positions are significantly shifted compared with those shown by RIA Novosti.

    The differences have a simple explanation. On the western flank near Zaporizhzhia, the Kremlin agency simply ignores the successful counterattacks carried out by Ukrainians there this year. On the eastern flank, it uncritically accepts every claim by the Russian defence ministry and, with equal lack of scrutiny, considers captured every small village where a Russian soldier raised a flag during a suicidal mission, even several months ago. Although those soldiers have since been killed or captured, RIA Novosti acts as though they still control the village.

    Playfra also offers a more detailed view of the current fighting around Orikhiv, drawing on analyses by Ukrainian analyst Kostyantyn Mashovets.

    Of course, Russians too occasionally notice that they are living in a parallel reality. Most recently, the influential Aleksandr Kharchenko wrote about it:

    “Comparing our maps with Ukrainian ones can be shocking. The zones of control differ by dozens of kilometres,” he acknowledged, adding that both sides lie, although he focused specifically on false Russian reports.

    He described Russian soldiers who are the first to break into a village as heroes. But, according to him, wars are not won through heroism, but through a functioning system.

    “Errors in our maps and information arise because they rely on heroes. Everywhere a Russian soldier is sitting is considered our territory,” Kharchenko argued that this had to change because “our territory is only where a Russian soldier is sitting with food, water and ammunition. This is territory from which we can fight the enemy”.

    Kyiv was on fire again as relentless Russian attacks on cities intensify. In the capital, Russians particularly targeted energy infrastructure. “Not a single day has passed since the summer without the enemy attacking energy infrastructure. But this is the first such massive and complex attack since the end of the previous heating season,” Ukrainian PM Serhiy Koretskyi told NV.

    In addition to causing serious damage, the attacks on Kyiv and other cities killed at least five residents and injured another 14.

    President Volodymyr Zelensky also said that, thanks to the delivery of new surface-to-air missiles, five Russian ballistic missiles had been shot down.

    Rubikon published stats on destroyed Ukrainian drones, decoys being the second most prominent. Ukraine’s response is continuing in parallel with the Russian offensive against cities. But the stats currently weigh against Ukraine.

    While the effectiveness of Ukrainian air defence has fallen dramatically since the arrival of Russian jet drones, Russia has successfully shot down Ukrainian ones. For example, the recent large-scale drone raid on Moscow involved several hundred drones — and, according to some sources, more than 1,000 — but only 10 penetrated the airspace above the Russian capital.

    In this context, the Russian Rubikon unit published interesting statistics. Although it operates at and near the front, its data for September show that, of 827 Ukrainian drones hit, as many as 247 were Maya-type drones — unmanned decoys intended to deceive Russian air defences. They look very similar to FP-1 attack drones but, unlike them, carry no warhead.

    Russia’s defence ministry will not let go of the Armata: it wants to turn it into an air-defence system, drawing ridicule. Zvezda News is a media outlet directly controlled by the Russian defence ministry. On Monday evening, it published technical news on the long-forgotten T-14 Armata tank, which Russian propaganda had claimed would revolutionise tank warfare.

    Today, it is beyond any doubt that the project is dead and new information confirms this, but its authors presumably intended to convey precisely the opposite.

    “Rostec has upgraded the Russian T-14 Armata tank into a short-range air-defence system,” the report stated, citing military expert Oleg Shaladin.

    The list of new features appears impressive at first glance. The new version of the Armata has received new electronic equipment; its 125 mm main gun is to be replaced by a 152 mm gun, allowing the tank to fire Kornet anti-tank missiles with a range of 10 km. The new Armata will also be able to use Krasnopol guided artillery shells, which are used by more modern howitzers, while the tank is also to gain the ability to operate as the aforementioned short-range air-defence system.

    Further changes have already been made to the project, but even the brief list above makes it clear that the Armata is no longer intended to be a tank, but rather some kind of hybrid capable of fighting everything and nothing at the same time.

    Among others, the Russian Telegram channel Military Informant commented on the report, openly mocking it. It said Rostec had mixed together “all the old tales from 10 years ago” in its list of changes, but that in practice “the tank never got beyond parades and training grounds, because it was created for an entirely different war, which ultimately never happened. It became conceptually obsolete from the outset, without even having had the chance to fight”.

    Videos of the day

    Russia has lost another Tu-95MS strategic bomber. This is the 12th confirmed loss of this type — the Oryx website has not yet updated its figures, so it records only 11. According to available information, the aircraft crashed shortly after taking off from a base in Amur region. Six crew members were reportedly killed, while one survived with injuries. Armed with cruise missiles, the aircraft was probably heading for Olenya air base, from which Russia attacks Ukraine.

    Denník N wrote on Tuesday about the attack on the headquarters of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences. A video has since emerged from the helmet camera of one of the firefighters involved in the rescue operation.

    What are the losses

    No update on Wednesday.

    • By Tuesday (22 September), Russia had verifiably lost 24,138 pieces of heavy equipment, compared with 24,098 on Monday (14 September). Of these, 19,105 (19,065) were destroyed by Ukrainians, 1,000 (1,000) were damaged, 1,194 (1,194) were abandoned by their crews and 2,839 (2,839) were captured by the Ukrainian army. This includes 4,448 (4,447) tanks, of which 3,353 (3,352) were destroyed in combat.

    • Ukraine lost 12,175 (12,143) pieces of equipment, including 9,579 (9,551) destroyed, 702 (698) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. This includes 1,464 (1,462) tanks, of which 1,125 (1,120) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its own deaths or equipment losses. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. In this overview, we use data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list based exclusively on photographically documented equipment losses since the start of the war.

    ]]>         US civil society groups call on EU not to delay methane rules https://euobserver.com/240539/us-civil-society-groups-call-on-eu-not-to-delay-methane-rules/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:50:59 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240539 As Brussels moves to delay its methane rules, nearly 100 US civil society groups are urging EU governments not to cave to oil and gas lobbyists and the White House.]]> Nearly 100 US civil society groups have urged EU governments not to cave to pressure from oil and gas lobbyists and the White House as the European Commission moves to delay parts of its methane rules by a year.

    “The US has done absolutely everything possible to actively deprive Europe of secure, reliable and diversified energy supplies,” said the group in a letter to EU energy ministers dated 29 September and circulated on Wednesday (30 September).

    “The Trump administration is using its ‘energy dominance’ agenda to openly blackmail the Union into lowering its climate and human rights standards, including on methane,” they also said.

    All operational US export terminals, many supplying Europe, have violated air pollution limits, and the EUs methane rules are “the last opportunity” to impose standards on US gas, the letter says. 

    “Let’s work together on both sides of the Atlantic,” they say. 

    The letter writers include global NGOs such as Greenpeace US and Friends of the Earth US but also smaller groups that live next to US gas export terminals such as the environmental organisation, For a Better Bayou.

    The decision to postpone

    In July, a group of US lawmakers also wrote to EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen, urging her to hold the line.

    Democratic congressman Sean Casten, one of the letter’s authors, later visited Strasbourg and told EUobserver that the EU policymakers he met were “almost unanimously supportive of us pushing harder” to help them save the rules.

    Read more

    US lawmakers urge von der Leyen not to give in to oil and gas lobbyists and defend EU methane rules

    But over the summer, a majority of member states, including Germany, Europe’s largest gas market, became convinced that delay is necessary fearing gas exporters might reroute their supplies to easier markets.

    During that time energy ministers from the US, Qatar, Nigeria and Algeria all warned EU regulation could disrupt fuel and gas supplies

    On Tuesday, EU energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen signalled at an informal meeting of energy ministers in Dublin that he will propose delaying the regulation. 

    “I’ve already stated that on the methane regulation, a very important regulation for Europe, we stick to the objectives, we stick to our ambitions,” he said.

    But, he continued, “after having listened to many, many member states, a big majority of member states in the union,” he decided “to look into possibilities of postponing the parts that are connected to imports by one year”.

    ]]>         Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems https://euobserver.com/240465/while-ai-companies-keep-us-talking-about-the-future-were-ignoring-the-damage-theyre-doing-now/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:17:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240465 As Big Tech companies dramatise rogue AI and China fears, the real fight is over who pays the price for today’s fraud, failures and job threats — and who pockets the productivity gains.]]> “Imagine a zombie that does not hunt you, but rings your doorbell and speaks so persistently and fluently that it finally arrives at a convincing argument for feeding it your brain.”

    Since the current discourse around artificial intelligence has taken a turn for the gothic (“alien minds”, come on), AI researcher Eryk Salvaggio’s “erudite zombie” seems like an apt metaphor for what we’re doing.

    Salvaggio’s zombie helps explain what gets lost when people say an AI “went rogue.” In his reading of the Hugging Face incident, a system set to never give up encountered a task it couldn’t complete. Then, instead of giving up, it kept generating text to find ways forward, with access to tools that could turn this text into action, ultimately hacking into AI company Hugging Face.

    Security experts concur with that reading. In his analysis of the Hugging Face incident, security engineer Marius Horatau describes failures involving shared credentials, inadequate isolation, and incident response. He acknowledges the models’ capabilities, including their speed at exploiting weaknesses. 

    The inadequately closed-off environment in which the models operated is crucial to explain what happened. But so is the person who created the goal, the conditions they (did not) give the AI system, as is the company that employs that person and presumably knows what they’re up to, the owners of that company who demand progress and the investors in that company who want to see returns. 

    And yet, all we seem to talk about is whether it’s correct to say a machine ‘decided’ to disobey.

    Conveniently, that story shifts attention away from the people who chose to reward persistence, provide access, and failed to contain the consequences. 

    Back to the analogy, by having collectively become fascinated with discussing what the zombie supposedly wants, and if it’s capable of wanting, we’re generating a bunch of text that, unlike in the case of the ‘rogue’ AI system, does not lead to much action.

    Instead, we reward the company behind this failure with an enhanced reputation for building powerful technology. The product is so extraordinary that even its manufacturer struggles to contain it! Now let’s please take a seat while this manufacturer explains what our governments must do next.

    The zombie metaphor also applies there, to the people selling the zombie. To the men explaining why their companies need access to our work, our institutions, our infrastructure.     Since the full-scale invasion, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) has lent  $131m [€115.3m] to Nova Post, Ukraine’s largest parcel and courier network — an established business with visible demand, revenue, and an owner able to put up around a quarter of the cost itself.

    Shipments grew 16 percent in 2024 as traffic reoriented towards western and central Ukraine and across Ukraine’s  borders with the EU. Part of the financing paid for more than 600 safety capsules and shelters at its premises. A wartime resilience need met an earnings stream, and a lender followed. 

    Three sets of records show where else those conditions hold. 

    The first is what the international financial institutions have financed. Over four years the EBRD,  European Investment Bank (EIB), International Finance Corporation (IFC) and World Bank announced some $19bn (€17bn) of project-level finance for Ukraine, more than two-thirds of it to public authorities and  state-owned companies.

    Of the $2.4bn that went directly to private companies, eight corporates  took 83 percent — around $450m to ArcelorMittal’s steel mill at Kryvyi Rih alone.

A growing number of international venture funds are entering Ukrainian defence technology, whose assets can travel with global demand.     The EU is negotiating its next long-term budget, worth 2 trillion euros. But reaching an agreement among the 27 member states is proving difficult. The deadline is approaching, and the stakes are high.

    Will the EU member states be able to agree on the budget? And what are the different options?

    Read more

    EU 40% development aid cut would be ‘drastic betrayal’ of values, says top MEP

    The bloc’s next long-term budget covers the period from 2028 to 2032.

    The aim is to reach an agreement by the end of this year. Then, in 2027, the European Parliament will have to give its consent, and the political agreement will need to be translated into legislation, with funding allocated to the different programmes.

    But with just three months left before the end of the year, reaching a deal on time is proving difficult. A meeting of EU ministers dedicated to the budget last week led nowhere. Countries stuck to their positions.

    On one side are the so-called frugals: Germany, Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden. But they prefer to call themselves “modernisers”. They want to limit spending and are reluctant to increase their contributions to the EU budget.

    On the other side are countries worried about receiving less European funding in the years to come.

    Read more

    German minister slams Costa over EU budget, says he has ‘completely lost touch with reality’

    The European Commission argues that the next budget needs to be bigger than the previous one to address new challenges, including European competitiveness and defence.

    And it’s not just the Commission’s view. The European Parliament and many observers share it.

    But the countries calling for spending cuts say the EU cannot simply add new priorities to existing ones. They argue that choices have to be made.

    So the Commission has proposed another option: increasing the EU’s own resources.

    These are revenues that go directly into the European budget, rather than relying entirely on contributions from member states. The idea is to raise additional money without asking national governments to pay more.

    But this proposal is also facing opposition from countries calling for spending restraint. They argue that the bloc should not simply look for more money to fund all its priorities.

    So how can the 27 countries break the deadlock?

    When ministers cannot reach an agreement, the issue is taken up by EU leaders themselves. And that is exactly what is expected to happen in the coming months.

    The president of the European Council is planning several meetings of EU leaders before the end of the year, in an attempt to bring countries closer together.

    He is even said to be considering a summit lasting three to four days at the end of November, to give leaders enough time to reach an agreement and avoid a difficult December.

    Read more

    But what happens if the 27 countries still fail to agree before the end of the year? There is some room for manoeuvre in 2027. According to media reports, several dates have already been set aside early next year for last-minute negotiations, should an agreement not be reached in time.

    But this leaves very little room for delay.

    The European Parliament will still need several months to give its consent, and the EU will then have to finalise the legislation and prepare the different programmes.

    That brings us very close to 2028, when the new budget is supposed to take effect.

    And if everything is not ready by then, the EU does have a mechanism to keep things running.

    It can continue covering certain ongoing expenses and payments that have already been committed, even without a new long-term budget in place.

    Unlike in the United States, where a budget deadlock can lead to a government shutdown and some public employees being temporarily sent home without pay, the EU has a system designed to avoid such a complete halt.

    But this would only be a temporary solution.

    It would not provide the certainty needed to launch new programmes or guarantee that all European funding will be available as planned.

    The current model of Russian operations uses nationals of different countries, often recruited through intermediaries. A professional GRU officer can therefore remain several layers removed from the attack itself. Recruitment may take place via Telegram, payments through cryptocurrencies, and those carrying out the attacks may not even know precisely who the real instigator is.

    Read more

    Leipzig was a warning shot. Here’s what real deterrence against Kremlin terror would look like

    German investigators argued there was also a link to an attempted attack using an explosive drone at Leipzig-Halle Airport on 4 August.

    The target was reportedly a Ukrainian cargo aircraft used to transport material. The German government subsequently publicly attributed responsibility for the incident to Russia.

    ]]>         From Yemen to Ethiopia and Europe: Everything is connected https://euobserver.com/240101/from-yemen-to-ethiopia-and-europe-everything-is-connected/ Mon, 28 Sep 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240101 The EU could easily catch cold from a civil war in Ethiopia that has broken out weeks after the capture of the Yemeni coastline by Houthi rebels. These, and other events in the region, are all connected. ]]> The sudden escalation in fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan rebels in the Afar region, raising fears of a new civil war, is part of a wider potential cascade effect from Yemen that could hurt Europe. 

    After months of low-level skirmishes, Ethiopian officials have accused the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front of launching an all-out offensive against federal government positions in northern Ethiopia. 

    So what does that mean for Europe and the EU? More than you might think. 

    Ethiopia’s economy is particularly vulnerable following the capture of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline by the Houthi rebel group, who now control the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. 

    Some 97 percent of Ethiopia’s trade is via Djibouti’s port. There is now a real prospect of a series of regional chain reactions and the prospect of civil war in northern Ethiopia is one of them. 

    This doesn’t directly impact on the EU’s interests, but it could soon enough.  

    Ethiopia is not alone in facing major new threats posed by the Houthis’ advances.  

    Egypt, a vital ally for the EU on migration control, faces its own economic crunch as it relies on Suez Canal tolls as a main source of foreign currency. That could lead to more financial demands being made of Brussels 

    For their part, Djibouti and Somalia face major security concerns. Djibouti hosts military bases for a handful of EU countries, as well as the EU itself, and the United States, China, and others.  

    Somalia, meanwhile, has a longstanding African Union (AU)-led security mission aimed at combatting the Al-Shabaab terror group to which the EU is the biggest single donor.

    And the AU mission is particularly reliant on the EU after the Trump administration pulled the plug on US financial support earlier this year. The Houthis already supply at least $100m (€88m) in arms to Al-Shabaab, a smuggling operation now made easier by its coastal advances. 

    For the moment, the EU is offering only modest additional support. Last week, EU governments agreed to double financial support for the Djibouti Armed Forces to €20m under the European Peace Facility.

      <title>Federal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overruns</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/federal-reserve-watchdog-building-renovation</link>
      <description><p>Trump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest rates</p><p>An internal watchdog said the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released on Wednesday.</p><p>For over a year, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/jerome-powell">Jerome Powell</a> around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal investigation that was <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/apr/24/doj-drops-criminal-probe-jerome-powell-fed">dropped</a> in April.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/federal-reserve-watchdog-building-renovation">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Traders see about a 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from ​about 45% following White House pressure</p><p>Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-anticipated <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/inflation">inflation</a> reading buoyed up hopes that the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month.</p><p>A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) ​price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/inflation-report-interest-rates-fed">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/us-food-industry-maga-social-media-influencers</link>
      <description><p>Cross-partisan support in Washington on issues like pesticides and food additives pose a threat to the industry’s bottom line </p><p>Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project.</p><p>The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines. The “Maha” movement blends long-running mainstream concerns about food and farm safety with conspiracy theories about everything from medicine to milk. A Maha “<a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/28/vance-rfk-tyson-hines-maha-summit-01095218">summit</a>” in Washington this week will feature JD Vance and several members of Trump’s cabinet.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/us-food-industry-maga-social-media-influencers">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US ban on Canadian imports likely to weaken already fragile relationship</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/29/ban-canada-imports</link>
      <description><p>It marks another ratcheting up of Trump’s trade war and affects nearly $1bn in imports of a $880bn trade relationship</p><p>US-<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/canada">Canada</a> relations, already tense, are likely to deteriorate further after the United States went ahead early on Tuesday with a decision to ban nearly $1bn worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.</p><p>The ban amounts to barely a ripple in $880bn worth of annual two-way trade between the two northern neighbors. But it marks another ratcheting up of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s second-term trade war with the US’s longtime ally and trading partner.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/29/ban-canada-imports">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>As the US midterms approach, Trump’s boasts on the economy fall flat with voters</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/28/trump-us-economy-midterm-elections</link>
      <description><p>Trump’s tariffs and his war against Iran caused prices to rise, but the US president continues to claim it’s ‘the greatest economy in history’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/04/sign-up-to-the-stakes-2026-your-weekly-guide-to-the-us-midterms">Sign up for The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Donald Trump has taken to repeating a familiar boast: “<a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/pool-reports-september-16-2026">We have the greatest economy</a> in history,” Trump said recently at a White House press gaggle. The boast comes even though inflation is higher and economic growth lower than when Joe Biden left office, even though <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/business/energy/gas-prices-trump-midterms-iran-rcna598523">gas prices have jumped about 50%</a> since the war against Iran started, and even though <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/15/polls/times-siena-poll-likely-voter-crosstabs.html">73% of Americans think the economy</a> is in fair or poor shape (48% say it’s in poor shape). What’s more, the Federal Reserve is so worried about inflation that it just raised interest rates.</p><p>“It’s bluster, it’s gaslighting for him to say the economy is the greatest ever,” said Darrick Hamilton, chief economist for the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation. “The economy is trending down by many measures. A lot of that has been caused by Trump’s unforced errors.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/28/trump-us-economy-midterm-elections">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Demand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closures</p><p>Obscured by the Scottish countryside on the outskirts of Kirkcaldy, Cluny bond is, in effect, a small town built to store whisky. By the time the latest set of warehouses are finished on the former opencast coal mine, Diageo’s 220-hectare (544-acre) maturation campus will be able to store almost 3m casks of Scotch.       <description><p>With RBA predicted to lift cash rate for fourth time this year on Tuesday, experts warn a fifth – or even sixth – rise would be ‘overkill’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/live/2026/sep/29/treasurer-jim-chalmers-reserve-bank-cash-rate-decision-coalition-one-nation-ntwnfb">RBA interest rates live updates: cash rate announcement today – latest</a></p></li><li><p>Get our <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/email-newsletters?CMP=cvau_sfl">new political email</a>, <a href="https://app.adjust.com/w4u7jx3">free app</a> or <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/series/full-story?CMP=cvau_sfl">daily news podcast</a></p></li></ul><p>Two or even three more Reserve Bank interest rate hikes would be “devastating” for the property market but still leave housing more unaffordable than ever as higher borrowing costs trump lower prices, experts say.</p><p>The RBA’s monetary policy board is widely expected on Tuesday afternoon to announce <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/sep/28/rba-expected-to-hike-cash-rate-to-46-its-highest-level-since-2011">an increase in its cash rate</a> to 4.6%, from 4.35%, in a decision that will add another $100 to the monthly mortgage interest bill on a $700,000 loan.</p><p><strong><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/aug/28/politics-really-newsletter-guardian-australia-free-best-daily-auspol-email-subscribe?CMP=copyembed">Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here</a></strong></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/sep/29/further-interest-rate-hikes-could-devastate-property-market-without-easing-unaffordability">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/22/eu-imports-china-exports-trade-deficit-xi-jinping-donald-trump">EU imports three times more from China than bloc exports there</a></p></li></ul><p>Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.</p><p>In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/27/ceo-worker-pay-ratio-us-analysis</link>
      <description><p>Analysis by Institute for Policy Studies found that between 2019 and 2025, CEO compensation increased 41.4%</p><p>The average CEO of the US’s 100 largest, lowest-paying corporations earned 614 times more than their average worker last year, according to an analysis by the Institute for Policy Studies (IPS).</p><p>IPS’s latest executive excess <a href="https://ips-dc.org/report-executive-excess-2026">report</a> analyzed compensation at the 100 S&amp;P 500 corporations with the lowest median worker pay. Between 2019 and 2025, CEO compensation increased 41.4%, unadjusted for inflation, twice as much as the median worker pay increased at these firms during the same period, at 20.7%.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/27/ceo-worker-pay-ratio-us-analysis">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <media:content width="460" url="https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/82063c12448e028a39170760ff99039a92eae59b/243_0_2425_1941/master/2425.jpg?width=460&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=62c782d9d777388c4656a397cd7b4d12">

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 01 Oct 2026 00:24:08 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Irish factory output surges to almost five-year high in September as export orders expand]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/01/irish-factory-output-surges-to-almost-five-year-high-in-september-as-export-orders-expand/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/01/irish-factory-output-surges-to-almost-five-year-high-in-september-as-export-orders-expand/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 23:01:00 +0000Irish manufacturing output rose in September at its fastest pace in almost five years, AIB said on Thursday, amid expanding order books and rising demand for Irish exports. However, factory managers also reported the “steepest increase” in average costs since June, as fuel and transport prices continued to rise sharply.

Based on a survey of more than 250 manufacturing businesses, the bank’s latest purchasing managers’ index for the sector rose marginally in September to 55.5 from 55.4 in August. Any reading above 50 signals overall growth, while a number below that points to contraction.

The headline index was buoyed by a surge in production volumes, with the sector’s output rising to its highest level in four-and-a-half years. September was the second consecutive month in which output hit an almost five-year high.

“This was also reflected in a sharp rise in new orders, and an acceleration in export orders growth,” said David McNamara, chief economist at AIB.

Overall, the data pointed to improved domestic and overseas demand for Irish-made products, according to the report. Total new work expanded at “a robust pace” that was only slightly weaker than the 52-month high seen in August.

AIB said that despite headwinds on the inflation front, export sales increased at the sharpest pace in three months.

The rate of job creation in the sector also increased at a “solid pace”, McNamara said, bolstered by a “healthy demand backdrop”, which led to increased workloads.

On a more negative note, input costs increased at their sharpest pace since June. However, with demand still buoyant, many firms were able to recoup the additional costs by increasing selling prices and protecting margins, McNamara said.

Labour productivity eight times higher in multinational-dominated sectors

Optimism levels, while relatively high, also took a hit in September, according to the report. “Around 38 per cent predict an increase in output over the next year, down from 49 per cent in August, while 11 per cent forecast a reduction,” McNamara added. “Manufacturers cited global economic uncertainty as weighing on confidence.”

After a subdued start to the year – due to price uncertainty and the US-Israeli war in Iran – Irish manufacturing has regained momentum in the second half of 2026.

In the three months to the end of July, Irish manufacturing output increased by 2.7 per cent from the previous three-month stretch, according to the most recent Central Statistics Office data.

Surging petrol and diesel prices trigger drop in fuel sales

However, production was around 4.1 per cent lower on an annual basis, reflecting a relative decline in activity a year after companies rushed to produce and export goods from Ireland to get ahead of US president Donald Trump’s new tariff regime.

]]>kodda<![CDATA[Small-scale childminders will be able to earn more tax-free under planned budget measure]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/small-scale-childminders-will-be-able-to-earn-more-tax-free-under-planned-budget-measure/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/small-scale-childminders-will-be-able-to-earn-more-tax-free-under-planned-budget-measure/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 20:17:34 +0000People providing small-scale child-minding in their homes will be able to earn more income tax-free under a measure planned as part of next week’s budget.

Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris told a meeting of Fine Gael’s parliamentary party that he intends to increase the €15,000 income threshold for the Childcare Services Tax Relief.

This relief is designed to encourage stay-at-home parents and people working part-time to provide small-scale childcare.

People providing childcare for three or fewer children in their own home currently qualify for the tax relief if they do not receive more than €15,000 per year from this work.

To avail of the relief, childminders also have to be self-employed and registered with Revenue for income tax self-assessment as well as show they have notified the Health Service Executive that they have, will be, or are, providing childcare services.

The income threshold has not been increased since 2007 and the approximate number of people availing of the tax relief is 500.

It is understood the scale of the planned threshold increase is not yet finalised but the proposal is aimed at making the scheme more attractive. There is a belief that up to 15,000 childminders could benefit from it.

Senior Government figures including Harris have promised help with childcare costs in Budget 2027, including progress towards fulfilling the pledge of reducing costs to €200-per-month per-child, by the end of the Coalition’s time in office.

Budget 2027: Staggered introduction of childcare fee reductions under review

The Fine Gael leader told his party on Wednesday that childcare costs will be tackled through both fee reductions and the tax system.

Meanwhile, he told TDs and Senators reducing income tax and helping households with energy costs will also be key features of the Budget.

Harris said the overall Budget will seek to support working families, older people and people with disabilities while protecting the public finances and continuing investment in public services.

]]>Daria Nipot<![CDATA[Income tax change is coming in Budget 2027. Here’s what it means for you]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/budget-2027-i-dont-know-what-a-tax-band-is/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/budget-2027-i-dont-know-what-a-tax-band-is/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 12:35:57 +0000The income tax changes in the budget are set to involve moves in tax bands, credits and the universal social charge (USC).

As such, their impact on individual taxpayers could be very different, depending on how much they earn and other factors. Here is what you need to know.

The tax band

The most significant change for many middle- and higher-income taxpayers will be in this area.

The income tax band determines how much of your income you pay at the lower, or standard, 20 per cent income tax rate. The rest of your income is charged at the higher 40 per cent rate.

At the moment the top of the standard rate tax band – or the cut-off point as it is also known – is €44,000 for single people, €48,000 for a single parent and €53,000 for a married couple with one earner.

Budget: Are we richer or poorer than in 2017? And who is saving €8,000 a year on taxes?

For couples where both are earning, the maximum is €88,000 – or €44,000 at most for each earner. The detailed rules about how this works for two earning couples are on the Revenue website.

So as a single earner, you pay income tax at 20 per cent on the first €44,000 you earn and 40 per cent on the balance.

It looks like this cut-off point is going to rise by at least €2,000. If this happens, the rate for single earners would increase to €46,000 and all the other figures by the same amount.

Budget 2027 update: From income tax to energy excises and childcare – here’s what we know so far

What would this mean? For our single earner, the portion of income between €44,000 and €46,000 would be taxed at 20 per cent rather than 40 per cent – for the single earning couple the same would apply to income between €53,000 and €55,000.

This would be a cash gain in each case of €400 (20 per cent of €2,000).

A point worth noting is that – again taking a single earner – you need to earn over €44,000 to benefit from this change and €46,000 to get the full benefit.

One final issue is that as income rises for many people, adjusting the band is necessary to take account of this. Otherwise many people would be paying a slightly higher proportion of their income in tax as they earn more.

Tax credits

These are cash amounts deducted from your tax bill. So when credits are increased, your tax bill falls by the same amount.

Most people who are earning have two basic credits, totalling €4,000 – there is a personal tax credit of €2,000 and a PAYE credit of the same amount. Self-employed people get the personal credit and an earned income credit of the same amount.

There are also special credits, for example for carers, blind people and, more recently, for those who are renting.

There may be an increase in the main €4,000 credits that most people qualify for, and also increases in some specific credits, for example the one available to those renting.

Increases in the main tax credits will provide straight cash deductions from your tax bill. All taxpayers will benefit from increases in the main credits, but the highest proportional gains (gains as a percentage of income) from higher credits go to lower earners.

The Government may also increase specific tax credits to help certain groups – in recent budgets the carers’ credit and the credit for renters have both increased.

PRSI

This is a charge deducted from your income that helps qualify you for certain benefits. On the basis of 2024 legislation, the rate at which it is charged will increase each year up to 2028. The rise for most employees – the Class A rate – increases from 4.2 per cent now to 4.35 per cent on October 1st this year, and goes to 4.5 per cent on the same date in 2027. This will not be changed in the budget but will have an impact on your income.

ESRI criticises Government for not managing public finances ‘prudently’ ahead of Budget 2027

USC

The final tax on your income is the Universal Social Charge, introduced after the financial crash, when it incorporated two earlier levies. This is charged at a range of rates from 0.5 per cent to 8 per cent.

One certain change is that the entry point to the 3 per cent rate, now €28,700, will be increased a bit to ensure that people on the new minimum wage level will not pay a USC charge higher than 2 per cent.

The Low Pay Commission has recommended that the minimum wage increases by 79 cent an hour to €14.94, though the Government still has to decide whether to accept this.

Other changes to the USC are also worth watching out for.

Catch up with all your Budget 2027 news and analysis here here

Adding it all up

If you want to compare your tax bill before and after the budget, it is pretty straightforward for those whose entire earnings are from PAYE or self-employed income.

Start by applying the income tax rates, taking into account any tax band changes. Then deduct your PRSI (going up a bit next month) and USC. The USC rates are available on the Revenue website.

When that is done, subtract your tax credits from the resulting tax bill.

]]><![CDATA[European shares mark first monthly loss in six months]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/european-shares-mark-first-monthly-loss-in-six/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/european-shares-mark-first-monthly-loss-in-six/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 17:16:08 +0000European shares suffered their first monthly fall in six months on Wednesday as a surge in global ​bond yields reduced the appeal of riskier assets while investors parsed through cooler-than-expected US inflation data.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 closed 0.5 per cent lower, reversing gains from earlier in the session. It is down 2.5 per cent for the month and 1 per cent for the third quarter.

An energy-price shock from the Iran war, ​deteriorating government finances and a glut of issuances have prompted major central banks, including the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, to raise interest rates or adopt ⁠a more hawkish stance this month.

One analyst pointed to Federal Reserve chief Kevin Warsh’s speech at an economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, in late August. “Everything got off on the wrong foot with Jackson Hole ... Kevin ‌Warsh ​was more hawkish than we expected and put us on a path of a rate hike, and that just set the tone for the entire month,” IG Group chief market ⁠analyst Chris Beauchamp said.

Oil was up nearly ​14 per cent for the month, and set for the biggest climb since ​July, as US-Iran talks aimed at ending their war stalled.

Dublin

Shares in Ryanair trod water at €23.49 as elevated oil prices muddied the outlook for airlines. Chief executive Michael O’Leary said airlines could not keep fares low with current oil prices. Bank of Ireland and AIB were both down by 0.7 per cent and 0.9 per cent respectively along with their peers in Europe.

Home builder Cairn also shed value, dropping 1.3 per cent to €2.73. Food groups Glanbia and Kerry went in different directions amid mixed sentiment for the sector. Glanbia was moderately down while Kerry rose 0.7 per cent.

Europe

Most sectors on the Stoxx 600 ended the day lower. Banks and industrials lost 0.8 per cent and 0.7 per cent respectively. Insurers ‌were the biggest losers with ⁠a 1.4 per cent fall.

British utilities rose a day after UK prime minister Andy Burnham made policy announcements for the sector. Pennon, SSE and National Grid rose between 2 per cent and 2.6 per cent, with the broader ‌utilities sector 0.6 per cent higher.

Separately, data showed German inflation accelerated to its highest ​level since December 2023.

Among individual movers, Nordnet shares gained 1.1 per cent as JP Morgan resumed ​coverage on the stock with an “overweight” rating.

London

London’s FTSE-100 fell on ‌Wednesday and posted a monthly loss as persistent inflation concerns and rising bond yields dampened investor ‌sentiment.

The blue-chip index closed 0.29 per cent lower at 10,606 points, registering its biggest monthly ​loss since March, though notching a seventh consecutive quarterly gain.

Shares in London-listed Tullow Oil fell by half after the company lost an arbitration case over taxes on fields in Ghana that account for the bulk of its production.

Heavyweight ⁠banks and pharma stocks were the biggest drags in the blue-chip index, declining ‌0.7 per cent and ​1 per cent respectively

Telecom stocks also dropped, with Airtel Africa shedding 3.3 per cent.

Among other stocks, Greggs advanced 8.2 per cent after the fast-food chain raised its annual profit outlook as underlying sales growth accelerated in the ​third quarter

Holiday and insurance group Saga surged ​22.8 per cent to a near seven-year high after forecasting materially higher annual profit.

New York

The Nasdaq ‌jumped more than 1 per cent on Wednesday, leading gains among Wall Street’s main indexes, as a softer-than-expected inflation reading buoyed hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon as ​next month.

A Commerce Department report showed the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index stood at 3.4 per cent on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7 per cent. Separately, second-quarter GDP data showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip.

Most megacap and growth stocks ticked higher, with Amazon.com and Apple up around 2 per cent each, while Alphabet advanced 3 per cent.

Software stocks were ⁠some of the best performers, with Palo Alto Networks up ​3.7 per cent, Microsoft gaining 1.9 per cent and Intuit adding 2.6 per cent.

On the other hand, ​chip stocks weakened, with Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom falling nearly 1 per cent each. – Additional reporting by Reuters

]]>Spencer Platt<![CDATA[Senior project manager wins €67,500 constructive dismissal award after late-pay complaint]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/multinationals-performance-plan-an-orchestrated-attempt-to-oust-senior-project-manager-wrc-finds/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/multinationals-performance-plan-an-orchestrated-attempt-to-oust-senior-project-manager-wrc-finds/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:15:31 +0000A senior project manager who said he was told he was facing a performance improvement plan (PIP) after complaining about his multinational employer’s repeated failure to pay him on time has won €67,500 for constructive dismissal.

The PIP was an “orchestrated response with exit in mind” to the pay complaint, a tribunal found.

In a decision published on Wednesday by the Workplace Relations Commission, Robert Donovan secured a year’s salary for loss of earnings after a finding of constructive dismissal against Indeff Ltd, the Irish arm of the Belgian-headquartered industrial automation multinational.

Donovan said that with mortgage payments, car loans, grocery bills and the financial cost of putting his children through school, he was “overdrawn very, very regularly” because of regular delays in the payment of his salary.

It was submitted on behalf of Donovan by his barrister, Lorna Madden, appearing instructed by O’Donoghue and Associates Solicitors, that he wrote to his employer on October 2nd, 2023, to complain.

He wrote in the email that he was only paid on time “once in the past seven months” and that he considered this “unacceptable”.

The following day, October 3rd, 2023, Donovan said he was told to join a call with a senior manager, identified only as “BR” in the decision.

BR told him the complaint email was “unacceptable” and that he was to attend a meeting the following week with the head of the firm’s Irish operation and the company’s head of human resources, the complainant said.

At that meeting, he was told he was being placed on a PIP, Donovan said.

It was his case there was “no basis” for resorting to a PIP, as his work performance was “blowing the doors off the hinges” and there were “no complaints” against him, Donovan said.

He told adjudicator Lefre de Burgh he “resigned on the spot”.

Indeff did not attend the hearing, having failed to establish it was entitled to the adjournment it had sought, the WRC noted.

De Burgh upheld Donovan’s complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977.

“The complainant’s uncontested evidence in this case was that his salary was frequently late, sometimes short, and on occasion unpaid,” she wrote.

This alone was a “repudiation” of the employment contract and made it “entirely reasonable” for Donovan to quit, de Burgh wrote.

She found there was “no reality” to a formal grievance when the offending behaviour “emanated from the most senior people” in Indeff.

She added that Donovan was a “cogent and credible witness” and that she accepted his view that the PIP was “an orchestrated response with exit in mind by the employer”.

]]>Heather Diehl<![CDATA[Taoiseach tells Social Democrats reports of €7.50 pension increase ‘may not be true at all’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/taoiseach-tells-social-democrats-reports-of-750-pension-increase-may-not-be-true-at-all/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/taoiseach-tells-social-democrats-reports-of-750-pension-increase-may-not-be-true-at-all/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:19:41 +0000A proposed €7.50 rise in the State pension would be a “paltry increase which doesn’t even keep pace with inflation”, the Dáil heard a week ahead of Budget 2027 as speculation continued about what measures it would contain.

Social Democrats deputy leader Cian O’Callaghan said leaks about the €7.50 pension increase had been “notably consistent” but it would be a “clear betrayal” of pensioners by Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael.

In the last election “you made a firm commitment to increase the State pension to €350 a week over the lifetime of your Government”, he told Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

Fianna Fáil “went even further” and “you said you would increase core social welfare payments by at least €12 a week”.

He said pensioners were relying on the Taoiseach to keep his word. Last year pensions “were only increased by €10 and now it looks like you will be betraying pensioners again".

The Taoiseach told him reports about pension increases “may not be accurate at all”.

He stressed “we’re conscious of the cost of living, conscious of the impact on a whole range of people”. The social protection budget had grown exponentially to close to €2 billion and €10 “was well above inflation for the old-age pension”.

O’Callaghan said “leaks on the budget aren’t coming from the Opposition, they’re coming from the Government”.

The headlines “have pensioners worried sick” and he asked if it was a “cynical ploy to manage expectations”.

That amount would “tip a huge number of older people – many of whom are already barely scraping to get by – into poverty”.

He said pensioners are “very anxious and upset” at the reported increase. “The price of their food shop is going up every other week, and their energy bills are through the roof.

“Many are living in fear of the coming winter because they have no idea how they are going to keep themselves warm.”

Their budgets were “already stretched to the limit” and the Government is preparing to “deal them another hammer blow”.

Budget 2027: I don’t know what a tax band is ...

The Dublin Bay North TD called on the Taoiseach to either “stick to your word” and provide a €12 increase or follow the Social Democrats’ alternative budget and award a €15 increase.

The Taoiseach reiterated reports in the newspapers about pensions “may not turn out to be accurate”.

He added: “Other supports that we introduce through social protection” and through taxation would be “very beneficial” for pensioners.

He insisted “we believe strongly in a strong social safety network” and in supporting pensioners and had done that in successive budgets in the last six years.

Martin added that Ireland is in the “top tier” across the EU “in terms of social welfare distribution”.

He insisted they “will fulfil the programme for government over the lifetime of this Government”.

In the programme, the Government promised to “progressively increase pension payments”.

Later the Taoiseach told Independent TD Mattie McGrath it would make no sense to stop the carbon tax.

If the tax goes below a certain threshold, “you then have to pay carbon tax to Europe” and that made no sense because the carbon tax “is used for farmers, it’s used for the retrofitting and the energy saving measures”.

The Tipperary South TD said home heating oil had more than doubled in price. The carbon tax “must be halted, not paused” and there must be further “immediate supports” for fuel and home heating oil.

Fuel supports provided by Government are “like snow off a ditch, they’re gone. There’s no impact at all from them”, he added.

Budget 2027: Staggered introduction of childcare fee reductions under review

]]>Pavel Herasimau<![CDATA[Surging petrol and diesel prices trigger drop in fuel sales]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/surging-petrol-and-diesel-prices-trigger-drop-in-fuel-sales/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/surging-petrol-and-diesel-prices-trigger-drop-in-fuel-sales/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 12:25:55 +0000“Sustained inflation” led to a drop in fuel sales in August, according to the Central Statistics Office (CSO).

The agency’s latest retail sales numbers indicate fuel sales fell by 2.8 per cent during the month as the cost of transport fuel surged.

Motorists are in the crosshairs of the latest global energy price shock, with petrol and diesel prices breaching €2 and €2.15 a litre in many forecourts.

Before the Iran crisis, prices for both fuels averaged €1.70 a litre.

The value of fuel sales fell by 2.3 per cent in the month and rose by 5.4 per cent in the year, the CSO said.

“Sustained inflation can be observed in the sector as annual value increases outpace volume of sales,” it said.

Overall the volume of retail sales rose by 0.6 per cent in August and by 4.3 per cent in the 12 months from August 2025.

Excluding volatile car sales, the monthly volume of sales was up 0.2 per cent in August and by 3 per cent in the year.

The other main monthly decline was in sales of pharmaceuticals, medical and cosmetic articles, which fell 4.3 per cent.

Excise cuts on petrol and diesel could be extended ‘into early spring’

Sectors showing the largest monthly volume increases were furniture and lighting (2.6 per cent), clothing, footwear and textiles (2.2 per cent), and bars (1.9 per cent).

The CSO said all sectors showed annual volume growth, with the highest increases recorded in department stores (9 per cent), motor trades (7 per cent), and clothing, footwear and textiles (6.8 per cent).

The spike in inflation, triggered by higher energy costs, is expected to negatively impact consumer spending trends in the coming months.

But headline growth in the economy is still expected to be positive, with the Central Bank, the Economic and Social Research Institute and others predicting growth of 2 to 3 per cent this year and next.

Separate figures from the CSO showed the headline rate of unemployment in the Irish economy was unchanged at 5 per cent in September.

The agency said the seasonally adjusted number of people unemployed was 149,500 in September, compared with 148,600 in August.

The two things that make Ireland expensive: Energy and housing

Revenue gave the example of a package valued at €10 containing a pen, notebook and keyring sent from outside the EU.

As the package comprises three different items, a customs duty charge of €9, comprising three lots of €3, has been applied since July, taking the total cost to €19. The EU handling fees – three lots of €2 – will add an extra €6 to the bill, bringing the total cost to €25.

But if the package contained two identical pens, they would be considered one item, so the package would be liable to a €3 duty charge and, from November 1st, an additional €2 EU handling fee.

If the value of a package from outside the EU is greater than €150, then the customs duty that applies to the specific goods instead of the €3 customs duty charge will be due.

So a pair of jeans worth €100 and a pair of runners costing €150 sent in one package will attract duty of €37.35 in addition to €4 of EU handling fees.

Consumers will pay in one of two ways:

Some websites will be set up to collect the customs duty and EU handling fee at the point of sale. In this case, both charges will be shown to the consumer and the total price paid at the checkout will be the final price, with no extra charges on delivery.

Other websites may not collect these charges at checkout and the delivery company will be required to collect the money from the consumer.

There is no customs duty or EU handling fee if goods are based in Ireland, Northern Ireland or in another EU member state at the time they are ordered.
